note: Fiscal size of the state as fractions of GDP/output. US block: OMB Historical Tables (FY2027 budget), federal FISCAL years; 1947-2025 actual, 2026 = OMB estimate published in the FY2027 budget. 'health' = Health + Medicare functions, 'incomeSecurity' = Income Security function, 'otherOutlays' = total outlays minus the named functions (incl. veterans, education, transport, offsetting receipts); 'otherReceipts' = excise + customs/other. 'stateLocal' = BEA state & local consumption expenditures and gross investment / GDP by CALENDAR year (2026 = mean of the 2 quarters published). CIV series: revenue = what the state collected; military + social + other = what it spent (outlays). Deficits ARE modeled where data exist (outlays may exceed revenue, e.g. world wars); judged samples assume a balanced budget (outlays = revenue). basis 'data' = IMF Public Finances in Modern History revenue/expenditure, GMSD (1816-1948) / SIPRI (1949-) military, Lindert/OECD social spending (decadal points before 1960 interpolated); 'other' = expenditure - military - social. Data windows: US/Britain/France/Spain/Denmark/Russia (incl. USSR) from 1816, Germany (holy_roman_empire) from 1871, Japan from 1860, China = PRC from 1949, India from 1947. Where a component has no data (e.g. revenue before the IMF series begins, social spending for Russia/China/India) the Jev-judged value is scaled to meet the data (ratio interpolated across gaps, fading out over 50 years before the data begin): basis 'blend'. 'judgment' = Jev Scores (fiscal reach, military share of spending, social provision, regulation) judged per civ at century marks, ends, anchor years and denser steps after 1800, interpolated to the sample grid and mapped to shares by a calibration fitted in code: per-level values start from a documented prior reading of each level and are pulled by ridge least squares toward the (civ, year) points where data exist and toward cited premodern anchors (Rome ~5% of GDP with the army 58-71% of spending; France 1700 ~5%, 1780 ~9%; Britain 1780 12%, 1810 18%, Elizabethan military 73-80%; Qing 1780 3-4%; early Ming government services 8.6%), then forced monotone. reach: levels -> 0.011, 0.019, 0.032, 0.042, 0.053, 0.082, 0.109, 0.330, 0.505 (fit on 54 data points + 7 anchors, rmse 0.40 in log units); military: levels -> 0.029, 0.035, 0.120, 0.561, 0.714, 0.714 (fit on 54 data points + 2 anchors, rmse 0.74 in logit units); social: levels -> 0.000, 0.001, 0.003, 0.005, 0.009, 0.094, 0.324 (fit on 48 data points + 0 anchors, rmse 0.45 in log units). 'regulation' (0..1, extra field) is the judged regulation of economic life. IMF segments contradicted by the military series were dropped as implausible: russia 1928-1940; japan 1875-1943; Germany 1913 dropped as a lone coverage outlier. IMF coverage breaks (central -> general government: France 1978, Germany 1970, Denmark 1971, Spain 1995, India 1988) are spliced by scaling the earlier 30 years by the break ratio, fading to 1 (basis 'blend'). US revenue 1902-1959 = Wallis (2000) national + state + local revenue rescaled to the IMF level over 1962-1992 (the IMF US revenue before 1960 is federal only). Industries: Jev Scores, probability-weighted level / (levels - 1). Actors: figures.json rulers/commanders/reformers with Wikidata P39 offices and years where found (else born+20 to death; 'years' says which), plus every US president 1945-2026 from Wikidata. Judgments are model evidence, not measurements; confidence = Jev confidence blended with 0.95 for data components.

reach.instructions: In `year`, how much of the economy's output did the government of `civilization.name` (in `civilization.region`) take in and command through taxes, tribute, rents, monopolies and labor dues? Judge the ruling state or states of this people in that year, using `civilization.about` and `peopleAliveThen`.
criteria: No regular taxation: a chieftain or war leader lives on tribute, plunder, gifts and personal dues from followers
Rulers live mainly from their own estates, booty and occasional tribute from subject peoples, with little regular tax
A palace, temple or loose kingdom takes a customary share of some harvests and labor service, but much of the land and trade lies beyond its reach
An agrarian kingdom or empire with a regular land or poll tax, but collection is thin, farmed out or skimmed by local lords, so little reaches the center
A strong centralized pre-industrial state: salaried officials collect land, poll and trade taxes across its territory and pay a standing army
An early modern fiscal-military state with permanent excise and customs duties, public debt and a large standing army or navy
An industrializing nation-state with income or property taxes and a professional civil service, but few social programs outside wartime
A modern bureaucratic state taxing incomes, payrolls and consumption, collecting a third or more of output and paying for pensions and health care
A total-war or central-planning state that commands most of the nation's output directly

military.instructions: In `year`, how much of what the government of `civilization.name` spent went to armies, fleets, fortifications and war, compared with its court, administration, debt, public works, religion and welfare?
criteria: Almost none: the state keeps no forces of its own beyond a few guards; its spending goes to the court, temples or civilian services
A small slice: large civilian budgets for pensions, health, schools and administration dwarf defense
Defense is one major item among several, alongside civil administration, debt service, public works or welfare
Defense is the largest single item, but the court, administration, temples or public building take much of the rest
Armies and war take most of what the state collects; the court, administration and public works share what is left
Nearly everything collected goes to warriors and war: the state is a war machine or fighting a total war

social.instructions: In `year`, what did the government of `civilization.name` provide for ordinary people's livelihoods: relief for the poor, the old, the sick and the hungry?
criteria: None beyond the ruler's household and retainers; the poor depend on kin and private charity
Occasional famine relief and alms given by rulers, temples or churches, with no regular public program
Regular public granaries, grain doles or temple redistribution for a capital city or for famine years
Organized poor relief funded by local taxes or church tithes in many localities
First social insurance laws: accident, sickness or old-age insurance for some workers, and public schooling
A broad welfare state: pensions, public schooling and health insurance cover most people
Universal pensions, health care and unemployment insurance, with cash transfers the largest part of state spending

regulation.instructions: In `year`, how much did the government of `civilization.name` regulate economic life: prices, wages, trades, markets, money and who may produce what?
criteria: Economic life is governed by custom and kin; rulers set no prices, wages, standards or trades
Rulers fix weights, measures, coinage and some tolls, but otherwise leave farming and trade alone
Law codes regulate contracts, debts, wages or prices in some trades, and the state monopolizes a few goods such as salt or metals
Guilds, licences, state monopolies and price controls govern many trades, enforced unevenly
Extensive mercantilist or bureaucratic control: state workshops, trade monopolies, export bans and detailed rules on crafts and commerce
A modern regulatory state: licensing, safety, labor, environmental and financial rules across most industries
Central planning: the state owns most enterprises and sets output, prices and wages

regulation.instructions: Today, how heavily do federal and state rules constrain how the `industry.name` industry in the United States operates (licensing, safety, environmental, financial, pricing and conduct rules)? `industry.about` describes it.
criteria: Almost no industry-specific rules: anyone can start, and only general business law applies
Light rules: registration, consumer-protection and workplace-safety law, but no licence is needed to operate
Moderate: specific safety, labeling or environmental standards with periodic inspections, but entry is open
Heavy: operating licences or permits, frequent inspections and detailed product, environmental or conduct rules shape daily operations
Very heavy: entry needs government approval, prices or capital are regulated, and dedicated agencies supervise firms continuously
Run by government itself: budgets, pay, prices and operations are set by statute, legislatures and agencies

capture.instructions: How much does the `industry.name` industry in the United States shape the rules that bind it, through lobbying, campaign money, revolving doors between its firms or unions and the regulators, and rules that protect incumbents from new competitors? `industry.about` describes it.
criteria: It has no organized influence; the rules are written without its input and it hardly lobbies
It lobbies through trade associations like most industries, but regulators and courts routinely overrule it
Significant lobbying and some revolving-door hiring win it narrow carve-outs and delays, but not the main rules
Heavy lobbying and campaign giving; its former executives staff the regulators and it largely writes the technical rules that govern it
The rules mainly serve incumbents: licensing, subsidies or tax breaks it secured keep out competitors, and its regulators rarely act against it
